dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — Waiting for the meeting to start
dialogs.intro: Bounmy and Budi chat about their schedules. Notice that the time is given with the part of the day, not as a 24-hour number.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ດຽວນີ້|Dǐao-nîi][ຈັກ|ják][ໂມງ|móong][ແລ້ວ|lèeo]

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເກົ້າ|Kào][ໂມງ|móong][ເຄິ່ງ|khòeng] [ປະຊຸມ|Pa-sum][ສິບ|síp][ໂມງ|móong]
lines.id: Half past nine. The meeting is at ten.
lines.literal: nine — o'clock — half. meeting — ten — o'clock.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຍັງ|Nyáng][ມີ|míi][ເວລາ|wée-láa] [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ຕື່ນ|tʉ̀ʉn][ນອນ|náwn][ຈັກ|ják][ໂມງ|móong]
lines.id: There's still time. What time do you get up?
lines.literal: still — have — time. you — wake — sleep — how-many — o'clock?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຫົກ|Hók][ໂມງ|móong][ເຊົ້າ|sâo] [ແລ້ວ|Lèeo][ກໍ|kaw][ອອກ|àwk][ກຳລັງ|kam-láng][ກາຍ|kaai][ໜ້ອຍ|nàwy][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng]
lines.id: Six in the morning. Then I exercise for a bit.
lines.literal: six — o'clock — morning. then — also — put-out — strength — little — one.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ຂະຫຍັນ|kha-nyǎn][ຫຼາຍ|lǎai] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຕື່ນ|tʉ̀ʉn][ເຈັດ|jét][ໂມງ|móong][ເຄິ່ງ|khòeng] [ບາງ|Baang][ເທື່ອ|thʉ̀a][ແປດ|pèet][ໂມງ|móong]
lines.id: You're so disciplined. I get up at half past seven. Sometimes at eight.
lines.literal: you — diligent — much. I — wake — seven — o'clock — half. some — times — eight — o'clock.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ກິນ|kin][ເຂົ້າ|khào][ສວຍ|sǔay][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ກິນ|Kin][ທຸກ|thuk][ມື້|mʉ̂ʉ] [ຢູ່|Yùu][ຮ້ານ|hâan][ໃກ້|kâi][ບ້ານ|bâan] [ຫຼັງ|Lǎng][ຈາກ|jàak][ນັ້ນ|nân][ຍ່າງ|nyàang][ມາ|maa][ອອບ|áwp][ຟິດ|fit]
lines.id: Every day, at a stall near my house. After that I walk to the office.
lines.literal: eat — every — day. at — stall — near — house. back — from — that — walk — come — office.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເລີກ|Lôek][ວຽກ|wîak][ຈັກ|ják][ໂມງ|móong]
lines.id: What time do you finish work?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຫ້າ|Hāa][ໂມງ|móong][ແລງ|léeng] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ຕອນ|tawn][ທ້າຍ|thâai][ເດືອນ|dʉan][ຊິ|si][ດົນ|dón][ກວ່າ|kwàa][ນັ້ນ|nân]
lines.id: Five in the afternoon. But at the end of the month it's usually later.
lines.literal: five — o'clock — evening. but — part — end — month — will — long — more — that.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຄື|Khʉʉ][ກັນ|kan] [ດຽວນີ້|Dǐao-nîi][ຫົວໜ້າ|hǔa-nâa][ກຳລັງ|kam-láng][ຖ້າ|thàa][ຢູ່|yùu] [ໄປ|Pai][ເນາະ|nāw]
lines.id: Same here. The boss is waiting now. Let's go.
lines.literal: same — together. now — head-front — (in-progress) — wait — (ongoing). go — okay?

notes: **ຈັກໂມງ ják móong = "what time," and ໂມງ móong = "o'clock" for a point in time.** Compare *ຊົ່ວໂມງ sùa-móong*, which means a length of time. *ສອງໂມງ* = two o'clock; *ສອງຊົ່ວໂມງ* = two hours.

**The part of the day is REQUIRED, because Lao uses a 12-hour clock.** *ຫ້າໂມງເຊົ້າ* (five in the morning) and *ຫ້າໂມງແລງ* (five in the afternoon) differ by one word at the end. Without it, people will ask you which one.

**ເຄິ່ງ khòeng = "half," and it goes AFTER the hour.** *ເກົ້າໂມງເຄິ່ງ* is literally "nine o'clock half" — half past nine, just as in English. ⚠️ Lao never counts toward the next hour the way German or Dutch "half ten" does.

**Minutes are given with ນາທີ *náa-thíi* after the hour**: *ສິບໂມງສິບຫ້ານາທີ* (ten fifteen). For "to," use *ອີກ ìik*: *ອີກສິບນາທີສິບໂມງ* (ten minutes to ten, literally "ten more minutes, ten o'clock").

**ກຳລັງ kam-láng = "in the middle of," and it goes BEFORE the verb.** It's often paired with *ຢູ່ yùu* at the end: *ກຳລັງຖ້າຢູ່* (is waiting). Either marker can be used alone, and in casual speech people more often use *ພວມ phuam*.

**ຫຼັງຈາກນັ້ນ lǎng jàak nân = "after that," and ແລ້ວກໍ lèeo kaw = "then."** Both link a sequence of activities. *ແລ້ວກໍ* is far more common in conversation; *ຫຼັງຈາກນັ້ນ* sounds tidier and is used when telling a longer story.
**ບາງເທື່ອ baang thʉ̀a = "sometimes."** Together with *ທຸກມື້* (every day), *ເລື້ອຍໆ lʉ̂ay-lʉ̂ay* (often), and *ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍ bàw khàwy* (rarely), these four words handle all frequency needs at A1.
**ຕື່ນນອນ tʉ̀ʉn náwn = "wake up," ເຂົ້ານອນ khào náwn = "go to bed."** Notice that *ນອນ náwn* on its own means both "sleep" and "lie down" — context separates them.
**ເລີກວຽກ lôek wîak = "finish work."** The word *ເລີກ lôek* means "stop, break up": *ເລີກຮຽນ* (school's out), *ເລີກແລ້ວ* (it's over).

grammars.title: Telling time: six parts of the day

head: Part of the day
Say it
Approx. hours
Example
rows: *ແປດໂມງເຊົ້າ* — 8 a.m.
*ສິບເອັດໂມງສວາຍ* — 11 a.m.
*ບ່າຍສາມໂມງ* — 3 p.m.
*ສາມທຸ່ມ sǎam thùm* — 9 p.m.

after: Notice that *ບ່າຍ* comes **before** the number (*ບ່າຍສາມໂມງ*), while the other parts of the day come **after** it (*ຫ້າໂມງແລງ*). That's the only odd placement, and it applies only to the afternoon.
For the night, Lao has its own unit: **ທຸ່ມ *thùm***, counted from 7 p.m. *ໜຶ່ງທຸ່ມ* = 7 p.m., *ສອງທຸ່ມ* = 8 p.m., *ສາມທຸ່ມ* = 9 p.m. You can also just use *ໂມງກາງຄືນ* and still be understood.

head: Lao
Say it
English
Position
Example
rows: *ຂ້ອຍກິນທຸກມື້*
*ບາງເທື່ອຂ້ອຍໄປ*
*ຂ້ອຍບໍ່ຄ່ອຍໄປ*
*ຂ້ອຍບໍ່ເຄີຍໄປ*

blocks.text: **ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍ *bàw khàwy*** is the most useful word here and the one most often misused. It isn't "not" but "not very," and Lao people use it to say no gently. *ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍແຊບ* (not very tasty) is far more polite than *ບໍ່ແຊບ* (not tasty), and it's often what they really mean.

sections.title: Time words that attach to every sentence

head: Lao
Say it
English
Lao
Say it
English
rows: ຕອນເຊົ້ານີ້

blocks.text: Lao time words can stand at the **start** or the **end** of a sentence, and they change nothing about the verb: *ມື້ອື່ນຂ້ອຍໄປ* and *ຂ້ອຍໄປມື້ອື່ນ* are both correct and both mean "I'm going tomorrow." Putting it first stresses the time a little more.

For "not yet," Lao uses **ຍັງບໍ່ທັນ *nyáng bàw than*** — literally "still not in time." *ຂ້ອຍຍັງບໍ່ທັນກິນ* = "I haven't eaten yet." In fast speech it's often shortened to just *ຍັງ*, and that's a complete answer.
